title: Why you forget things the second you walk through a door
hook_line: You walked into a room and forgot why.

beats.narration: You walked into a room and forgot why. And no, it's not your age.
It's the door. Scientists can actually make this happen on purpose, and the reason is kind of beautiful.
Quick question. How many times has this happened to you this week? Be honest.
At Notre Dame, psychologist Gabriel Radvansky had people carry objects through rooms. Some walked through a doorway. Others walked the same distance without one.
The doorway group forgot more about what they were carrying. Same walk. Same time. Just a door. It even worked in real rooms, not only on a screen.

Here's why. Your brain doesn't record life like one long video. It cuts it into scenes, and a doorway is a scene break. Your brain closes the old scene to make room for the new one, and your little mission gets filed away with it.
And here's the weird part. Going back into the first room didn't bring the memory back. The scene was already closed.
To be fair, a 2021 study found this shows up mostly when your mind is juggling a lot. So on a busy, stressed day? The door wins.
The fix is tiny. Right before you cross, say the goal out loud. Charger. One word carries it into the new scene with you.
So next time, don't blame your brain. Blame the door. Because you walked into a room and forgot why.

sources.finding: Walking through doorways increased forgetting in virtual and real rooms; returning to the original room did not restore memory (Radvansky, Krawietz & Tamplin, QJEP 2011).
Doorways did not always cause forgetting; effects appeared mainly under high memory load.
